title: December Lifts Your Revenue. It Quietly Lifts Your Stock Losses Too.
linkedin:
Black Friday is behind us. Christmas trading is ramping up. Revenue for the next five weeks is about to look very healthy.

It usually does.

Here's what rarely gets mentioned in the same breath: the same extra volume lifting revenue also lifts something else, the rate at which stock quietly goes missing.

Breakage. Miscounts. A pick that goes out against the wrong line. None of these show up as a line item on an invoice. They sit quietly inside cost of goods sold until the next physical stock count forces the gap into a number, weeks or months after the fact.

Here's the maths that makes this worth watching. A business doing $500,000 in revenue over the Christmas period, where shrinkage quietly rises from around 1 percent of sales in a normal month to 2 percent during the volume surge, is looking at the difference between a $5,000 leak and a $10,000 one. On an 8 to 10 percent net margin, that's a material share of the month's actual profit, gone before a single discount or wage cost is even considered.

Your bookkeeper will record that variance accurately once it's counted. Spotting the drift while it's still happening is a different job entirely, and it's usually the one nobody is assigned.

The businesses that keep this leak small check stock against sales at least once during the peak, not just at the next scheduled count.

Quick one for retailers and hospitality owners heading into Christmas: have you ever compared your stock loss rate in a quiet month against a flat-out one like December?

Most businesses never check, because it doesn't show up anywhere until the next stocktake. But the maths is sneaky: on a $500k December, shrinkage creeping from 1% to 2% of sales is a straight $5,000 hit to profit, before any discount or overtime cost even gets a look in.

It's not about anyone doing the wrong thing. More stock moving through the business just means more chances for something to go missing along the way.

Worth a spot check before the madness properly kicks in?

On a business doing half a million dollars across the Christmas period, a shift from around 1 percent stock loss in a normal month to 2 percent during the rush is the difference between a $5,000 leak and a $10,000 one, a meaningful chunk of a typical month's profit.

The businesses that keep this small do one simple thing: they check stock against sales once during the peak, not just at the next scheduled count.
